questions.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i+j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=49{cos}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(49{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(1)\cdot (-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{3}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-98{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{0}-98{u}^{2}\,du \\  & =(98\operatorname{sin}⁡t-7\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=xy\,i+{x}^{2}\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =xy=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=4{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(4{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1}-16{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =30{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =30{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1\,\text{d}t \\  & =30(2\pi -0) \\  & =60\pi \end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:

$$
x=8\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =4x=4(8\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=32\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =4y=4(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=24\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-8\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(32\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(24\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-8\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }192({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }192\,\text{d}t \\  & =192t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =192(2\pi -0) \\  & =384\pi \end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =9{x}^{3}=9{cos}^{3}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{cos}⁡t=u,du=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(9{cos}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{1}^{1}(u+{u}^{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(x-16y)\,i+(x+y)\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=16.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $1,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x-16y=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =x+y=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4{cos}^{2}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\,\text{d}t \\  & =4t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =4(2\pi -0) \\  & =8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=3x\,i+3y\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=64.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3x=12\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =3y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24{cos}^{2}⁡t+24{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24\,\text{d}t \\  & =24t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =24(2\pi -0) \\  & =48\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{3}\,i+{x}^{3}\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={1}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{3}={sin}^{3}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{3}={cos}^{3}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({cos}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({sin}^{2}+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(y-x)\,i-(x+y)\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={3}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y-x=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-(x+y)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-9(2\pi -0) \\  & =-18\pi \end{aligned}
$$

{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={4}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $4.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-2x=-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})=-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}

$$

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = (y - x)\,\mathbf{i} - (x + y )\,\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = 4\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 4\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = 4\cos t, \qquad
	y = 4\sin t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y-x=4(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t), \\ Q(x,y) & =-(x+y)=-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-16t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-16(2\pi -0) \\  & =-32\pi \end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf{i} + x^2\,\mathbf{j}$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $9x^2 + y^2 = 9.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{1^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{3^2} = 1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} +3\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos t, \qquad
y = 3\sin t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =xy=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{2}={cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\cos t, \textrm d u = -\sin t\,\textrm d t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }9\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }10\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{1}^{1}10{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(-2)\cdot (\frac{t}{2})-(t)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}-2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =-16-0 \\  & =-16\end{aligned}
$$
